hits.title: Graphs which are vertex-critical with respect to the edge-chromatic class
hits.text: The edge-chromatic number of graph G is denoted by \(\chi '(G)\). A multigraph G is EN-critical (VN-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and \(\chi '(G-e)<\chi '(G)\) for all edges e in G \((\chi '(G-v)<\chi '(G)\) for all vertices v in G). A multigraph G is EC-critical (VC-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and G-e is Class 1 for all e in G (G-v is Class 1 for all v in G). For simple graphs EN-critical and EC-critical are equivalent. In this paper a number of interesting results and conjectures are given regarding multigraphs which are EN-critical but not EC- critical, regarding the relationship between VN-critical and VC-critical graphs and the relationship between VC-critical and EC-critical graphs.

hits.title: Which graphs have Hall number two?
hits.text: The paper brings a collection of so-called Hall-\(2^+\)-critical graphs, i.e. graphs with Hall number at least three all induced subgraphs have Hall number at most two. The authors relate this study to the question for which graphs the chromatic and choice numbers coincide. They furthermore conjecture that the constructed family provides full characterization of Hall-\(2^+\)-critical graphs by means of forbidden induced subgraphs.

hits.title: On the choosability of some graphs
hits.text:
Summary: Suppose \(\mathrm{ch}(G)\) and \(\chi(G)\) denote, respectively, the choice number and the chromatic number of a graph \(G= (V,E)\). If \(\mathrm{ch}(G)= \chi(G)\) then \(G\) is said to be chromatic-choosable. Recently, \textit{J. A. Noel} et al. [J. Graph Theory 79, No. 2, 86--102 (2015; Zbl 1320.05045)] proved a conjecture by \textit{K. Ohba} [ibid. 40, No. 2, 130--135 (2002; Zbl 1004.05030)] that states that \(G\) is chromatic-choosable whenever \(|V(G)|\leq 2\chi(G)+ 1\). Here, we present other classes of chromatic-choosable graphs that do not satisfy the hypothesis of the proven conjecture.

 Moreover, we give the upper bounds for the choice numbers of the Mycielski graphs and the Cartesian product of any two graphs, in terms of a vertex-neighborhood condition.

hits.title: Hall \(t\)-chromatic graphs
hits.text: Summary: A graph is Hall \(t\)-chromatic if there is a proper list-multicoloring of the graph from a constant list of cardinality \(t\) whenever the graph together with that constant list assignment and the ``color demand'' function that prescribes the cardinalities of the color sets, satisfy Hall's condition. We show that every graph is Hall \(t\)-chromatic for \(t\leq 2\), and that a great many familiar graphs, including the bipartite graphs and the complete multipartite graphs, are Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t\). However, it turns out that there exist graphs that are not Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t\) sufficiently large.

hits.title: Estimates of the choice numbers and the Ohba numbers of some complete multipartite graphs.
hits.text: The Ohba number of a graph \(G\) is defined as the smallest integer \(n\) such that the join \(G\vee K_n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ch}(G\vee K_n)=\chi (G\vee K_n)\), where \(\operatorname{ch}(G)\) and \(\chi (G)\) are the choice number and chromatic number of \(G\), respectively [\textit{K. Ohba}, J. Graph Theory 40, No. 2, 130--135 (2002; Zbl 1004.05030)]. In this paper, some estimates of the choice numbers and Ohba numbers of the complete multipartite graphs \(K(m,n,1,\dots ,1)\) and \(K(m,n,2,\dots ,2)\) are given for various values of \(m\geq n\geq 1\). For example, for complete \(k\)-partite graphs we have \(\operatorname{ch}(K(m,n,1,\dots ,1))\leq n+k-1\), \(\operatorname{ch}(K(m,2,\dots ,2))\leq 2k-1\) and equality holds for \(m\geq {{2k-2}\choose {k-1}}^{2}\).

hits.title: Note on Hall \(t\)-chromatic spectra
hits.text: Summary: A method for investigating the Hall \(t\)-chromatic spectrum of a graph is introduced and used to show that each graph in a certain collection, including every Mycielski graph from the Grötzsch graph, has the minimum Hall \(t\)-chromatic spectrum \(\{0,1,2\}\).

hits.title: Progress on the Hall-number-two problem
hits.text: The paper is concerned with the Hall number \(h(G)\) of simple graphs \(G\), which may be considered as a variant of the list-chromatic number (alias choice number) \(c(G)\) of \(G\). For basic definitions and results the reader should consult the second and third author's papers [Extending Hall's theorem, in: Topics in combinatorics and graph theory, 359-371 (1990; Zbl 0731.05017), Discrete Appl. Math. 94, No. 1-3, 227-245 (1999; Zbl 0934.05001), and \((*)\) Congr. Numerantium 121, 161-182 (1996; Zbl 0897.05040)]; in particular the last one is cited more than once in the paper. The Hall-number-two prolem (as indicated in the title) means the problem to characterize the class of graphs with Hall number at most 2. Having a forbidden-induced-subgraph characterization in mind the authors contribute a lot of new items to the list of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs started in \((*)\). But up to now a final characterization is not obtained.

The present second edition of this popular book for talented high school students and also for mathematicians contains mostly the material of the first edition. The contents of the first edition is outlined in the report (1991; Zbl 0727.52001).

The second edition is expanded by the following five short chapters. Chapter 5 (five pages) recalls two theorems by \textit{D. Karabash} [Geombinatorics 16, No.~2, 262--265 (2006)] on rectangles that can be tiled by L-tetrominoes of the same orientation in such a way that the tiling has \(2\)-fold symmetry. Chapter 6 (five pages) presents some results on three-dimensional tromino tilings of a cube obtained mostly by \textit{N. Starr} [Geombinatorics 18, No.~2, 72--87 (2008; Zbl 1184.05020)]. Graph Theory 13, No.~1, 97--98 (1989; Zbl 0661.05044)] and \textit{B. D. McKay} and \textit{S. P. Radziszowski} [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 69, No.~2, 193--209 (1997; Zbl 0860.05043)].

Chapter 8 (four pages) gives information on the progress in the research on the famous Borsuk problem after the first edition of this book; the story of finding counterexamples. Starting from the well-nown result by \textit{J. Kahn} and \textit{G. Kalai} [Bull. Am. Math. Soc., New Ser. 29, No.~1, 60--62 (1993; Zbl 0786.52002)] and finishing by the result of \textit{A. Hinrichs} and \textit{C. Richter} [Discrete Math. 270, No.~1--3, 137--147 (2003; Zbl 1028.52012)] on the counterexample in \(E^{298}\), which (till now) is the space of the lowest known dimension for which the Borsuk problem has a negative solution. 

Chapter 9 (twelve pages) discusses the following problem of E. Nelson (1950): which is the smallest number \(\chi\) of colours sufficient for colouring the plane in such a way that no two points of the same colour lie apart at unit distance. After recalling the proofs by E. Nelson (1950) and J. Isbell (1950) that \(4 \leq \chi \leq 7\), the author presents results on the \(n\)-colouring of a given type and on the almost chromatic number \(\chi_a\); see the paper by \textit{I. hits.title: The chromatic numbers of some Euclidean distance graphs
hits.text: For \((X,\rho)\) a metric space and \(s>0\), let \((X,s)\) be the graph whose vertices are the points of \(X\), with \(x\) and \(y\) adjacent precisely when \(\rho(x,y)= s\). In this paper, \(X\) is usually a subset of some Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(\rho\) the usual Euclidean metric. The authors study the chromatic number of \((X,s)\). They present some results, particularly for \(n= 2\), and they state six open problems.

hits.title: On the chromatic numbers of some 3-uniform hypergraphs in the plane
hits.text: Let \(\mathbb R^2\) be the real plane. In this paper, the authors determine upper bounds for the chromatic number of some special \(3\)-uniform hypergraphs \((\mathbb R^2, S)\).

hits.title: Thwart numbers of some bipartite graphs
hits.text: The choice number \(c(G)\) of a graph \(G\) is the least integer \(l\) such that if each vertex of \(G\) is assigned a list of \(l\) colours, then there must be a proper vertex colouring of \(G\) from these lists. For an integer \(k\) at least the chromatic number of \(G\), let \(c_k(G)\) be defined as for \(c(G)\) except that only a total of \(k\) distinct colours may appear on the vertex lists. The thwart number of \(G\) is the least \(k\) such that \(c_k(G)= c(G)\). This paper surveys what is known concerning thwart numbers, and obtains results on the thwart number of very `unbalanced' complete bipartite graphs, and on graphs with thwart number 3.

hits.title: The structure of a type of affine primitive non-synchronizing groups
hits.text: Summary: The study of synchronizing groups has been the forefront research in permutation group theory. In this paper we study the generalized Paley graphs and discuss the condition of the equality between the clique number and chromatic number of the generalized Paley graphs. Then, we prove that the generalized Paley graphs is isomorphic to the orbital graphs of a certain affine groups, and discuss the synchronization property of a certain affine group. Furthermore, we use this property to construct a type of primitive non-synchronizing groups.

hits.title: Point-variety incidences, unit distances and Zarankiewicz's problem for algebraic graphs
hits.abstract: In this paper we study the number of incidences between $m$ points and $n$ varieties in $\mathbb{F}^d$, where $\mathbb{F}$ is an arbitrary field, assuming the incidence graph contains no copy of $K_{s,s}$. We also consider the analogous problem for algebraically defined graphs and unit distance graphs. First, we prove that if $\mathcal{P}$ is a set of $m$ points and $\mathcal{V}$ is a set of $n$ varieties in $\mathbb{F}^{D}$, each of dimension $d$ and degree at most $Δ$, and in addition the incidence graph is $K_{s,s}$-free, then the number of incidences satisfies $I(\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{V})\leq O_{d,Δ, s}(m^{\frac{d}{d+1}} n+m)$. This bound is tight when $s,Δ$ are sufficiently large with respect to $d$, with an appropriate choice of $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}(m,n)$. We give two proofs of this upper bound, one based on the framework of the induced Turán problems and the other based on VC-dimension theory. In the second proof, we extend the celebrated result of Rónyai, Babai and Ganapathy on the number of zero-patterns of polynomials to the context of varieties, which might be of independent interest. We also resolve the problem of finding the maximum number of unit distances which can be spanned by a set of $n$ points $\mathcal{P}$ in $\mathbb{F^d}$ whose unit-distance graph is $K_{s, s}$-free, showing that it is $Θ_{d,s}(n^{2-\frac{1}{\lceil d/2\rceil +1}})$. Finally, we obtain tight bounds on the maximum number of edges of a $K_{s, s}$-free algebraic graph defined over a finite field, thus resolving the Zarankiewicz problem for this class of graphs.

hits.title: Coloring of \(G^2\setminus G\), for Euclidean graph \(G\)
hits.text:
The text: Graph \(G=(V(G),E(G))\) is called Euclidean if and only if \(V(G)\) is a finite subset of \(R^2\) and \(\{x,y\}\in E(G)\) if and only if \(\text{dist} (x,y)\leq d\) where \(d\in R\) is fixed. Let \(S(G)=G^2 \setminus G\). The vertex set of \(S(G)\) is \(V(G)\) and there is an edge \(\{x,y\}\) in \(E(S(G))\) if and only if \(\{x,y\}\notin E(G)\) and \(x,y\) have a common neighbor in \(G\). We consider vertex coloring of the graphs \(S(G)\), where \(G\) is Euclidean.

 Problem. Is there a polynomial algorithm, which gives the chromatic number of \(S(G)\) for Euclidean graphs \(G\)?

 The problem appeared in telecommunication. In practical applications standard approximate algorithms are used, but they do not use the geometric properties of \(S(G)\) and they seem not to be the most effective one. For geometric reasons \(\chi(S(G))\leq 12\), where \(G\) is Euclidean, but on the other hand it is difficulty to find Euclidean graphs \(G\) such that \(\chi(S(G))>6\).

hits.title: Finite analogues of Euclidean space
hits.text: Let \(\mathbb{F}_q\) be the finite field with \(q=p^r\) elements for \(p\) an odd prime. Define a ``distance'' on \(\mathbb{F}^n_q\) by \(d(x,y)={^t(x-y)}(x-y)\) for column vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb{F}^n_q\) and join two vertices \(x,y\in\mathbb{F}^n_q\) by an edge iff \(d(x,y)= a\), where \(a\in\mathbb{F}_q\) is fixed. This defines a graph \(E_q(n,a)\) associated with \(\mathbb{F}^n_q\). For \((q,n,a)\neq(q,2,0)\) with \(-1\) not a square in \(\mathbb{F}_q\), the graph \(E_q(n,a)\) is a connected regular graph of known degree (see Theorem 1). The eigenvalues of the adjacency operators can be expressed in terms of Gauß sums and generalized Kloosterman sums. If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of the adjacency operator with \(\lambda\) different from the degree of the graph, then Weil's estimate for Kloosterman sums yields \(|\lambda|\leq 2q^{(n-1)/2}\). From this it is not hard to prove that for \(n=3\) many of the above graphs are Ramanujan and many are not Ramanujan. It is further shown that for fixed \(q\) and \(n\) the set of graphs \(E_q(n,a)\) splits into very few isomorphism classes. Hence, these finite Euclidean graphs differ from the graphs constructed for the non-Euclidean finite upper half plane. -- The paper is illustrated by some beautiful plots in Mathematica.

hits.title: $2$-quasi-perfect Lee codes and abelian Ramanujan graphs: a new construction and relationship
hits.text: Summary: This paper presents a new explicit infinite family of 2-quasi-perfect $p$-ary Lee codes of length $\frac{q-1}{2}$ and dimension $\frac{q-1}{2}-2k$ for $q = p^k \ge 14$, $p\geq 5$ a prime. hits.title: Finite upper half planes over finite fields
hits.text:
This paper extends results of the author, N. Celniker, S. Poulos, the reviewer, C. Trimble and E. Velasquez on finite upper half planes over finite fields of odd characteristic to finite fields of characteristic 2. The properties of these graphs were discussed in a series of papers. See the reviewer's article [Exp. Math. 5, 15-32 (1996)] for a survey on this subject for fields of odd characteristic. In the survey we also consider finite Euclidean graphs. More details can be found in the author, \textit{S. Poulos}, the reviewer, \textit{C. Trimble} and \textit{E. Velasquez} [Contemp. Math. 173, 15-70 (1994; Zbl 0813.11034)].


The finite upper half plane graphs were created in an effort to find a finite model of the Poincaré upper half plane similar to the finite model of the circle given by \(\mathbb{Z}/n \mathbb{Z}\), viewed as a circle graph. Let \(\mathbb{F}_q\) be a field of odd characteristic. Fix \(\delta\) a non-square in \(\mathbb{F}_q \). The finite upper half plane \(H_q\) consists of points \(x + y \sqrt \delta\) with \(x,y\) in \(\mathbb{F}_q \) and \(y \neq 0\). If \(\mathbb{F}_q\) has even characteristic, one replaces \(\sqrt \delta\) with a root of some irreducible quadratic over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). Just as in the real case if \(g = {a \;b \choose c \;d}\in GL(2, \mathbb{F}_q)\), we can see that \((az + b)/(cz + d)\) is in \(H_q\) if \(z\) is in \(H_q\). Thus one can identify \(H_q\) with \(G/K\), if \(K\) is the subgroup of \(G\) which fixes \(\theta\).


There is an analogue of the Poincaré distance defined by \(d(z,w) = {N(z - w) \over \text{Im} z \text{Im} w}\), where if \(z = x + y \theta\), with \(x,y \in \mathbb{F}_q\), we set \(y = \text{Im} z\). And the norm of \(z\) is \(Nz = z \overline z\), where \(\overline z = x + y \overline \theta\), where \(\overline \theta\) is the other root of the irreducible quadratic satisfied by \(\theta\); i.e. \(\overline \theta = \theta^q \). The distance is \(G\)-invariant.


Fix \(a \in \mathbb{F}_q\). The graph \(X (\theta, a)\) has as vertices the elements of \(H_q\) and two vertices \(z,w\) are connected by an edge if \(d(z,w) = a\). If \(a \neq 0\) or \(T^2 - 4N\), where the irreducible quadratic satisfied by \(\theta\) is \(x^2 - Tx + N\), the graph has degree \(q + 1\). Over \(\mathbb{F}_4\), the author finds that the icosahedron occurs as one of these graphs. In general many of the graphs are isomorphic. If \(a \neq 0\) or \(T^2 - 4N\), the graphs are connected by Theorem 3.4 of the paper.


Theorem 2.10 of the paper shows that the graphs \(X (\theta, a)\) are highly regular and thus one can collapse the adjacency matrix to a \(q \times q\) matrix with the same eigenvalues. See \textit{B. Bollobás} [Graph Theory, Springer (1979; Zbl 0411.05032), p. 159]. Many facts about the collapsed adjacency matrix are proved; e.g., that the entries are among the numbers 0, 1, 2, and \(q + 1\), while any given row has at most 2 entries equal to 1. These results were proved by \textit{S. Poulos} [Ph. D. Thesis, UCSD (1991)] for fields of odd characteristic. Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 show that the girth and diameter of a connected finite upper half plane graph is at most 4. Then conditions are given that determine when 3 occurs.


One object of the work is a study of the spectra of adjacency matrices. In particular one asks: Are the graphs \(X (\theta, a)\) Ramanujan in the sense of \textit{A. Lubotzky}, \textit{R. Phillips} and \textit{P. Sarnak} [Combinatorica 8, 261-277 (1988; Zbl 0661.05035)]? This means that if \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix with \(|\lambda |\neq q + 1\), is it true that \(|\lambda |\leq 2 \sqrt q\)\ ? Such graphs are best possible expanders among \((q + 1)\)-regular graphs as the number of vertices goes to infinity. Here, of course, as \(q\) goes to infinity, so does the degree. Another property of Ramanujan graphs is that the simple random walk on \(X (\theta, a)\) converges particularly rapidly to uniform. Other references for the subject include \textit{A. Lubotzky} [Discrete groups, expanding graphs and invariant measures, Prog. Math. 125 (1994; Zbl 0826.22012)] and \textit{P. Sarnak} [Some applications of modular forms, Cambridge Tracts Math. 99 (1990; Zbl 0721.11015)].


For odd characteristic, the graphs were proved to be Ramanujan using work of \textit{J. Soto-Andrade} [Proc. Symp. Pure Math. 47, 305-316 (1987; Zbl 0652.20047)] and \textit{N. Katz} [J. Reine Angew. Math. 438, 143-161 (1993; Zbl 0798.11053)]. For fields of even characteristic the graphs were proved to be Ramanujan by \textit{R. Evans} [Finite Fields Appl. 1, 376-394 (1995; Zbl 0844.11078)] and \textit{N. Katz} [Finite Fields Appl. 1, 395-398 (1995; see following review)]. See also \textit{Winnie Li} [Astérisque 228, 101-120 (1995; Zbl 0844.11076)] for estimates of the exponential sums involved (in odd characteristic). Li does not require \(\ell\)-adic étale cohomology. Instead she uses A. Weil's proof of the Riemann hypothesis for zeta functions of function fields associated to curves.


Finally the author shows that for \(a \neq 0\) or \(T^2 - 4N\), if \(q \neq 3\), the complement of the graph \(X (\theta, a)\) is Ramanujan. And he proves that for fields of even characteristic, 0 is not an eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix.

hits.title: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem over certain fields
hits.abstract: We compute the Hadwiger-Nelson numbers $χ(E^2)$ for certain number fields $E$, that is, the smallest number of colors required to color the points in the plane with coordinates in~$E$ so that no two points at distance $1$ from one another have the same color. Specifically, we show that $χ(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})^2) = 2$, that $χ(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})^2) = 3$, that $χ(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{7})^2) = 3$ despite the fact that the graph $Γ(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{7})^2)$ is triangle-free, and that $4 \leq χ(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{11})^2) \leq 5$. We also discuss some results over other fields, for other quadratic fields. We conclude with some comments on the use of the axiom of choice.

hits.title: On a generalization of the Hadwiger-Nelson problem
hits.abstract: For a field $F$ and a quadratic form $Q$ defined on an $n$-dimensional vector space $V$ over $F$, let $\mathrm{QG}_Q$, called the quadratic graph associated to $Q$, be the graph with the vertex set $V$ where vertices $u,w \in V$ form an edge if and only if $Q(v-w)=1$. Quadratic graphs can be viewed as natural generalizations of the unit-distance graph featuring in the famous Hadwiger-Nelson problem. In the present paper, we will prove that for a local field $F$ of characteristic zero, the Borel chromatic number of $\mathrm{QG}_Q$ is infinite if and only if $Q$ represents zero non-trivially over $F$. The proof employs a recent spectral bound for the Borel chromatic number of Cayley graphs, combined with an analysis of certain oscillatory integrals over local fields. As an application, we will also answer a variant of question 525 proposed in the 22nd British Combinatorics Conference 2009.

hits.title: On chromatic number of unit-quadrance graphs (finite Euclidean graphs)
hits.abstract: The quadrance between two points A_1=(x_1, y_1) and A_2=(x_2, y_2) is the number Q (A_1, A_2) = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2. Let q be an odd prime power and F_q be the finite field with $q$ elements. The unit-quadrance graph D_q has the vertex set F_q^2, and X, Y in F_q^2 are adjacent if and only if Q(A_1, A_2) = 1. Let χ(F_q^2) be the chromatic number of graph D_q. In this note, we will show that q^{1/2}(1/2+o(1)) <= χ(F_q^2) <= q(1/2 + o(1)). As a corollary, we have a construction of triangle-free graphs D_q of order q^2 with χ(D_q) >= q/2 for infinitely many values of q.

hits.title: Pell-type equations over algebraic number fields
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 21, No. 3, 707-712 (2026)
hits.text: Summary: Let \(K\) be an algebraic number field, let \(\mathcal{O}_K\) be its ring of integers, and let \(D\in\mathcal{O}_K\) be non-square in \(K\). The solutions of \(X^2-DY^2=1\) with \(X,Y\in\mathcal{O}_K\) are identified with the norm-one units of the quadratic order \(\mathcal{O}_K [\sqrt{D}]\). This yields an explicit group law and the signature formula \[\text{rank}\,\mathcal{P}(K,D)=r_2(K)+t(K,D),\] where \(t(K,D)\) counts the real embeddings \(\tau:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}\) for which \(\tau(D)>0\). The formula gives criteria for finiteness and rank one. In the rank-one case, every solution is generated by a fundamental relative unit up to torsion, and its coordinates satisfy explicit linear recurrences.

hits.title: Representations of uniformly hyperfinite algebras and their associated von Neumann rings
On some classes of non-Archimedean operator algebras
hits.source: Shamseddine, Khodr (ed.), Advances in ultrametric analysis. Selected papers based on the presentations at the 12th international conference on \(p\)-adic functional analysis, Winnipeg, MB, Canada, July 2--6, 2012. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society (AMS) (ISBN 978-0-8218-9142-1/pbk; 978-1-4704-1024-7/ebook). Contemporary Mathematics 596, 133-148 (2013).
hits.text:
This paper deals with some classes of algebras of operators on a non-Archimedean Banach space \({\mathcal B}\) over a complete non-Archimedean and non-trivially valued field \(K\).

A bounded linear operator \(A\) on \({\mathcal B}\) is called \textit{strongly normal} if \(A\) is normal and its spectrum is a non-empty totally disconnected compact subset of \(K\) that coincides with the spectrum of the Banach algebra generated by \(A\) and the unit operator. Strongly normal operators play an important role in non-Archimedean quantum mechanics.

In Section 2, the author proves that orthoprojections on \({\mathcal B}\) (i.e., norm-one projections) and multiplication operators on non-Archimedean Banach spaces of continuous functions are strongly normal.

The purpose of Section 3 is to construct a non-Archimedean counterpart for the classical class of von Neumann algebras. This is done via the following reduction procedure. Let \({\mathcal U}\) be an algebra of operators on the \(K\)-Banach space \(c_0(J,K)\) (\(J\) an infinite set) of all \((x_j)_j \in K^{J}\) such that \(x_j \to 0\). Denote by \({\mathcal U}_1\) and \({\mathcal U}_0\) the closed and open unit balls on \({\mathcal U}\), respectively. The \textit{reduced algebra} \(\tilde{{\mathcal U}} = {\mathcal U}_1 / {\mathcal U}_0\) can be considered as a \(\tilde{K}\)-algebra, where \(\tilde{K}\) is the residue class field of \(K\). Then the class of algebras \({\mathcal U}\) for which \(\tilde{{\mathcal U}} \) is a Baer ring is the desired one. The main reason to choose Baer rings is that for them there is a (purely algebraic) theory which is parallel to the theory of von Neumann algebras. This construction, together with the theory of Baer rings developed by \textit{I. Kaplansky} [Rings of operators. York-Amsterdam: W.A. Benjamin, Inc. (1968; Zbl 0174.18503)], lead to a kind of classification of these ``non-Archimedean von Neumann algebras''.

Finally, Section 4 is devoted to construct and study some operators on the non-Archimedean Banach space of continuous functions \(S \times G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}_p\), where \(S\) is a totally disconnected compact Hausdorff topological space, \(G\) is an abelian infinite second-countable totally disconnected compact Hausdorff topological group acting transitively on \(S\) by homeomorphisms, and \(\mathbb{C}_p\) (\(p\) a primer number) is the completion of the algebraic closure of the field of \(p\)-adic numbers. The author pays special attention to crossed products, the non-Archimedean couple of one of the most important methods to construct von Neumann algebras in the classical case. This results in a class of algebras \({\mathcal U}\) whose reduced algebra \(\tilde{{\mathcal U}}\) is a type \(I\) Baer ring.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1273.00050].

hits.title: Pythagorean triples: uniform distribution and geometrical applications. II
hits.text:
The first part of this article appeared in [Acta Math. Inform. Univ. Ostrav. 11, No. 1, 29--72 (2003; Zbl 1169.11306)]. In this earlier paper the author continued his investigation on Pythagorean triples, uniform distribution and applications which he already started in [Bonn. Math. Schr. 121, 1--32 (1980; Zbl 0444.10025) and in [Aequationes Math. 58, No. 1-2, 163--175 (1999; Zbl 0938.11037)]. 

In the first part of this paper the author focused on the construction of Pythagorean triples by means of prime numbers in the Gaussian number field and various geometric applications. In the first three sections of Part I applications to line geometry and to spherical trigonometry are discussed. Sections 4--6 are devoted to rotations in the three-dimensional space. 

The present second part starts with Sections 7, which is devoted to the orthogonal group in higher dimensions. Section 8 gives applications to non-Euclidean geometry and in Section 9 Clifford's surface is discussed. In Section 10 Gödel's cosmological model is considered. In Section 11 and 12 applications to a probabilistic model and to infinite series are discussed. The paper ends with several interesting remarks on solitons, Doppler's phenomenon and aberration and on extensions of the theory to quaternions and imaginary quadratic number fields.

hits.title: Coefficient quantization in Banach spaces
hits.text:
Let \((e_i)\) be a sequence in a (separable) Banach space \(X\). The authors consider the problem of approximation an element \(x\in X\), for a given \(N\), by an element of the `lattice' \(\mathcal{D}^N(e_i)=\{\sum_{i\in E}2^{-N}k_i e_i:k_i\in \mathbb{Z},\;E\subset \mathbb{N}\;\mathrm{finite}\}\). One of the main results is the perhaps surprising fact that roughly speaking, `quantization' of the unit ball for some \(\varepsilon>0\) automatically implies `quantization' of the whole space. A consequence of this is that, given \(\varepsilon>0\), every separable infinite-dimensional Banach space \(X\) admits a sequence \((e_i)\) contained in its unit ball such that the additive group generated by \((e_i)\) is \(1/(3+\varepsilon)\)-separated and \(1/3\)-dense in \(X\). 

The set \((e_i)\) has the \textit{Coefficient Quantization Property} (CQP) if, for each \(\varepsilon>0\), such that, for every finite \(E\subset \mathbb{N}\) and for every \(x\) with support contained in \(E\), there exists \(y\in\mathcal{D}^N(e_i)\) supported in \(E\) such that \(\|x-y\|\leq\varepsilon\). The main result of the paper: A separable Banach space \(X\) has a fundamental and total bounded biorthogonal system with the CQP if and only if it contains an isomorph of \(c_0\).

The paper was motivated by results on approximation of bandlimited functions by quantized coefficients [\textit{I.\,Daubechies} and \textit{R.\,De Vore}, Ann.\ Math.\ 158, No.\,2, 679--710 (2003; Zbl 1058.94004)] and results on quantization of finite-dimensional frames [see, e.\ g., \textit{J.\,J.\thinspace Benedetto, A.\,M.\thinspace Powell} and \textit{Ö.\,Yilmaz}, Appl.\ Comput.\ Harmon.\ Anal.\ 20, No.\,1, 126--148 (2006; Zbl 1088.42018)].

hits.title: Connectedness of the fibers of a Liouvillian function
hits.source: Publ. Res. Inst. Math. Sci. 33, No. 3, 465-481 (1997).
hits.text: Let \(f_1, \dots, f_p\) be irreducible analytic functions defined in a neighborhood of the origin in \({\mathbb{C}}^n.\) Then \(f = f_1^{\lambda_1} \cdots f_p^{\lambda_p}, \lambda_i \in {\mathbb{C}},\) is a multivalent function germ. Suppose that the unit is not contained in the additive group generated by the exponents \(\lambda_i.\) Then the range of \(f\) belongs to the quotient of \({\mathbb{C}}^\ast\) by the multiplicative group generated by \(\exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}\lambda_i), i = 1, \dots, p.\) Thus, analogs of the notions of Milnor fibration and regular fibers of \(f\) are well-defined [\textit{E. Paul}, Ann. Inst. Fourier 45, No. 1, 31-63 (1995; Zbl 0819.32014)]. The author describes sufficient conditions on the exponents \(\lambda_i\) under which the fibres of \(f\) are connected. In fact, he generalizes the corresponding results of \textit{D. Cerveau} and \textit{J. F. Mattei}, `Formes intégrables holomorphes singulières', Astérisque 97 (1982; Zbl 0545.32006), and some others obtained in the holomorphic (univalent) case.

hits.title: Paradigmatic motivic analysis
hits.source: Mazzola, Guerino (ed.) et al., Perspectives in mathematical and computational music theory. Osnabrück: Electronic Publishing Osnabrück (EPOS) (ISBN 3-923486-57-X/pbk; 3-923486-58-8/CD-ROM). Osnabrück Series on Music and Computation 1, 343-365 (2004).
hits.text:
Summary: Paradigmatic Motivic Analysis (PMA) aims at finding, classifying and, thereby, helping to understand structural relations within the variety of subsets of a single or between those of different musical pieces. According to Mathematical Music Theory as developed by G. Mazzola, a paradigm is determined by the geometric transformations from a suitably chosen subgroup of the affine group acting on the ambient space, describing the so-called Gestalt, in which the piece is modeled. The particular point of view taken here reduces a given musical melody to a (finite) set of rational points in the affine plane (the components of a point being onset and pitch), which are strictly ordered by their first components. Moreover, choosing the positive generator of the additive group generated by all onset differences of the notes occurring in the melody to be analyzed as a unit, the points in the plane can be assumed to have integer coordinates. Then, for a single melody the PMA investigates the inner symmetries of a finite set of points with integer coordinates in the affine plane, not two of which lie in a vertical line. An inner symmetry with respect to a given subgroup \({\mathcal G}\) of the planar affine group is constituted by a pair of subsets of the melody, each containing at least two points, for which there exists a transformation in the group \({\mathcal G}\) mapping one subset onto the other. Starting from this set of symmetry pairs we introduce several numerical and other characteristics, each intended to grasp pieces of information concerning symmetry and measure its extent within a melody.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1063.00008].

hits.title: From natural numbers to quaternions. Translated from the German by the authors
hits.source: Springer Undergraduate Mathematics Series. Cham: Springer (ISBN 978-3-319-69427-6/pbk; 978-3-319-69429-0/ebook). x, 285~p. (2017).
hits.text:
This book presents the classical construction of integers, rational, real (and \(p\)-adic), complex and quaternion numbers from the set of natural numbers, which are described by the Peano axioms (the German edition was reviewed in [Zbl 1279.00021]). This is not done in a strict axiomatic sense; for example, already in the first chapter on natural numbers, the logarithm and the Riemann zeta function are used in connection with the distribution of prime numbers. Each chapter presents the necessary means for constructing the new numbers, in particular homomorphisms and quotient groups as well as Cauchy sequences and valuations. Finally, each chapter has numerous exercises. The book is easy to read and well suited for undergraduates.

The following list of (mostly minor) deficiencies is longer than in most reviews; this is due to the fact that the reviewer is convinced of the importance of telling our students how the numbers that we are using in calculus have evolved and how they are constructed nowadays.

The most serious omission is not giving \textit{E. Landau}'s classical text [Grundlagen der Analysis. (Das Rechnen mit ganzen, rationalen, irrationalen, komplexen Zahlen.) Ergänzung zu den Lehrbüchern der Differential- und Integralrechnung. Leipzig, Akademische Verlagsgesellschaft (1930; JFM 56.0191.01)] as a reference; an English translation is also available [Zbl 0042.27803]. In his book, Landau presents the construction of these number systems (he does not discuss \(p\)-adic numbers or quaternions) with utmost elegance and clarity. The authors also do not address Landau's discussion of a gap in the naive definition of addition of natural numbers (given on p. 10 in the present book). On the other hand, the reference to \textit{A. Weil}'s [Basic number theory. 2nd ed. Berlin: Springer (1973; Zbl 0267.12001)] should be omitted since every undergraduate (and quite a few graduate students as well) will be frustrated should they pick up this high-brow introduction to class field theory.

On p. 9, the authors quote Kronecker by saying that God made the integers; by not giving the second part according to which all else is the work of man they seriously misrepresent Kronecker's statement. Kronecker was striving for an arithmetization of analysis; it is not important whether the natural numbers come from God or from Peano, what was important for him is that calculus (and ultimately the whole field of mathematics) is reduced (as far as possible) to theorems on natural numbers.

The polynomial characterization of prime numbers by Jones et al. in Theorem A1 via the famous polynomial in 26 variables is incorrect as stated; a much simpler polynomial that represents all primes is the polynomial \(f(x) = x+1\). The crux of the matter is the ``only if''-part of the statement.

In Remark 1.26, the construction of the integers is motivated by the ``desire to have a solution to the equation \(n + x = m\)''. This does not explain why negative numbers were invented before symbolic algebra, and in fact is simply not true, just as complex numbers (see p. 183) were not introduced for the want of solutions of the equation \(x^2 + 1 = 0\). As someone once said, mathematicians also did not feel the need to solve the equation \(x + 1 = x\).

Divisibility of natural numbers in Definition 2.1 is restricted to integers \(b \ne 0\). This not only complicates the statement of the fundamental properties of divisibility in Lemma 2.4, it also creates a gap in the Definition 4.1 of the greatest common divisors of two numbers not both equal to \(0\); similarly, Euclid's Lemma 1.7. in Chapter III uses divisibility for general integers. In Definition 2.7, it must be explained why we are not counting \(1\) among the prime numbers. In Exercise 2.12 the readers are asked to show that not every prime number (in particular \(5\)) occurs in the sequence of primes constructed in Euclid's proof, but the procedure given in the exercise does not coincide with the one in Euclid's proof (the latter produces the Euclid-Mullen sequence, in which \(5\) does occur).

The historical comments are distributed unevenly. Amicable numbers are credited to the Pythagoreans (this was first done by Iamblichos around 300 AD, that is, about 800 years after Pythagoras), the fundamental theorem of arithmetic is not attributed to anyone, and the prime number theorem is credited ``in a rudimentary form'' to Gauss, neglecting the contributions of Legendre. After proving Fermat's little theorem it is claimed that Euler generalized it to the case of products \(pq\) of two primes, whereas the general case is said to derive from Lagrange's theorem; but of course the result that \(a^{\phi(m)}-1\) is divisible by \(m\) whenever \(a\) and \(m\) are coprime is due to Euler.

The unique factorization theorem in Chapter I is proved directly and then used for deriving Euclid's Lemma, the existence of greatest common divisors and finally division with remainder. The reader should be told right away that it is also possible (and quite common) to proceed in the other direction. Similarly, the remarks on p.~95 seem to suggest that using Euclid's Lemma for proving unique factorization works only in the integers and not in the natural numbers.

The proof on p. 131 that curves of degree \(2\) with a rational point can be parametrized does not work for singular curves such as \(y^2 = 2x^2\). Although the authors go on to discuss the group of rational points on elliptic curves, the much simpler group law of rational points on the unit circle (or conics) is not mentioned.

In Section IV.5, the authors construct a bijection between the real numbers and the points on the number line. To this end, they assume that the Euclidean line satisfies a number of axioms. Perhaps the beginners would have appreciated a couple of comments as to what, if anything, goes wrong if we replace the Euclidean line by a line in finite fields or in the completion of the \(p\)-adic number field.

The sketch of the proof of Abel's theorem on the unsolvability of the general quintic by radicals given on p. 205 is not enlightening at all since it is not clear where the sketch goes wrong if we replace the degree \(5\) by \(4\) or \(3\); in fact, the notion of a solvable group is only introduced afterwards.

hits.title: On the unit sum number of some rings.
hits.text: Summary: The unit sum number, \(u(R)\), of a ring \(R\) is the least \(k\) such that every element is the sum of \(k\) units; if there is no such \(k\) then \(u(R)\) is \(\omega\) or \(\infty\) depending whether the units generate \(R\) additively or not. We show that if \(R\) is the ring of integers of a quadratic or complex cubic number field then \(u(R)\geq\omega\), in the quadratic case \(u(R)\) is completely determined. We also investigate tensor products of algebras. If the ground field is not the field of two elements then their unit sum number is 2 when at least one of them is algebraic and at least \(\omega\) when neither is algebraic and one of them is pure transcendental.

hits.title: Unit sum numbers of right self-injective rings.
hits.text: Summary: In a recent paper [\textit{D. Khurana, A. K. Srivastava}, J. Algebra Appl. 6, No. 2, 281-286 (2007; Zbl 1116.16033)] we proved that every element of a right self-injective ring \(R\) is a sum of two units if and only if \(R\) has no factor ring isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) and hence the unit sum number of a nonzero right self-injective ring is 2, \(\omega\) or \(\infty\). In this paper we characterize right self-injective rings with unit sum numbers \(\omega\) and \(\infty\). We prove that the unit sum number of a right self-injective ring \(R\) is \(\omega\) if and only if \(R\) has a factor ring isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) but no factor ring isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\), and also in this case every element of \(R\) is a sum of either two or three units. It follows that the unit sum number of a right self-injective ring \(R\) is \(\infty\) precisely when \(R\) has a factor ring isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\). We also answer a question of \textit{M. Henriksen} [J. Algebra 31, 182-193 (1974; Zbl 0285.16009), Question E, p. 192] by giving a large class of regular right self-injective rings having the unit sum number \(\omega\) in which not all non-invertible elements are the sum of two units.

hits.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for unit graphs to be Hamiltonian
hits.text:
Given an associative ring \(R\), the unit graph \(G(R)\) has the elements of \(R\) as the vertices and vertices \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent if \(x + y\) is a unit of \(R\). The following summary result is proved about associative rings and unit graphs. Theorem: Let \(R\) be a ring such that \(R \neq Z_2\) and \(R \neq Z_3\). Then the following are equivalent: {\parindent=6mm
\begin{itemize}\item[(a)] The unit graph \(G(R)\) is Hamiltonian. 
\item[(b)] The ring \(R\) cannot have \(Z_2 \times Z_3\) as a quotient. 
\item[(c)] The ring \(R\) is generated by its units. 
\item[(d)] The unit sum number of \(R\) is less than or equal to \(\omega\). 
\item[(e)] The unit graph \(G(R)\) is connected.


\end{itemize}}

hits.title: On unit sum numbers of rational groups.
hits.text:
We say an associative ring \(R\) has the \(n\)-sum property if every element of \(R\) can be written as a sum of exactly \(n\) units in \(R\). The unit sum number is then defined as \(\text{usn}(R)=\min\{n\mid R\) has the \(n\)-sum property\}. If every element of \(R\) is a sum of units but \(R\) does not have the \(n\)-sum property for any \(n\), define \(\text{usn}(R)=\omega\), and if \(R\) contains an element which is not a sum of units, set \(\text{usn}(R)=\infty\). Further define the unit sum number of an Abelian group or module to be that of its endomorphism ring. There has been a large amount of research on the subject of which Abelian groups and modules have unit sum number 2 and the properties of their endomorphism rings. However, until now it has not been known if there even exists a group with a finite unit sum number larger than 2.

 In the current paper unit sum numbers of rational groups (subgroups of the rational numbers under addition) are investigated. A notable feature of these groups is that if 2 is not a unit in the endomorphism ring, then the unit sum number is \(\omega\). Several other results are discussed by considering the number and distribution of rational primes which are, or are not, automorphisms of the group. The authors establish their main result using a combination of algebraic and number theoretic methods: the existence of rational groups with a finite unit sum number greater than 2.

hits.title: A survey of rings generated by units.
hits.source: Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse, Math. (6) 19, Spec. Issue, 203-213 (2010).
hits.text:
The research topic surveyed arose from the result of K. G. Wolfson and D. Zelinsky from the 50's that every linear transformation of a vector space over a division ring but the two-element space is the sum of two units. Many surprising results have been found since then, such as construction of a von Neumann regular algebra in which not all elements are sums of units; and that the matrix algebra of at least \(2\times2\) matrices over any ring has unit sum number 3, that is, all elements are sums of exactly 3 units, due to \textit{M. Henriksen } [J. Algebra 31, 182-193 (1974; Zbl 0285.16009)].

 The following research areas are described in detail: von Neumann regular rings generated additively by units; right self-injective rings generated additively by units; endomorphism rings of variously conditioned modules, such as (quasi) injective modules, generated additively by units; unit sum numbers of variously conditioned rings such as right self-injective rings and rings of integers. Furthermore, generalization of the problem with regular elements instead of units (which coincide in von Neumann regular rings) is also surveyed, and several open problems are propounded.

hits.title: Sums of units in function fields
hits.text:
Let \(R\) be a ring (with identity). An element \(r\) is called \(k\)-good if \(r=e_1+\cdots+e_k\), with \(e_1, \ldots, e_k \in R^*\). If every element of \(R\) is \(k\)-good we call also the ring \(k\)-good. The unit sum number \(u(R)\) is defined as \(\min\{k : R \text{ is } k\text{-good}\}\). If the minimum does not exist but the units generate \(R\) additively we set \(u(R)=\omega\). If the units do not generate \(R\) we set \(u(R)=\infty\).

In this paper the author considers the unit sum number for function fields. Let \(K\) be a perfect field and \(F/K\) an extension of transcendence degree \(1\), \(S\) a finite set of places of \(F/K\) and \(\mathcal O_S\) the ring of \(S\)-integers, then the author proves various results for \(u(\mathcal O_S)\). The first main result generalizes a theorem due to \textit{M. Jarden} and \textit{W. Narkiewicz} [Monatsh. Math. 150, No. 4, 327--332 (2007; Zbl 1121.12002)]. In particular the author proves that in any case we have \(u(\mathcal O_S)\geq \omega\). The second main result gives a characterization for all quadratic extensions \(F/K(x)\) with \(u(\mathcal O)=\omega\), where \(\mathcal O\) is the integral closure of \(K[x]\) in \(F\).

hits.title: The unit sum number of some projective modules.
hits.text:
Summary: The unit sum number \(\mathbf u(R)\) of a ring \(R\) is the least \(k\) such that every element is the sum of \(k\) units; if there is no such \(k\) then \(\mathbf u(R)\) is \(\omega\) or \(\infty\) depending whether the units generate \(R\) additively or not. If \(_RM\) is a left \(R\)-module, then the unit sum number of \(M\) is defined to be the unit sum number of the endomorphism ring of \(M\).

 Here we show that if \(R\) is a ring such that \(R/J(R)\) is semisimple and \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) is not a factor of \(R/J(R)\) and if \(P\) is a projective \(R\)-module such that \(JP\ll P\), then \(\mathbf u(P)=2\). As a result we can see that if \(P\) is a projective module over a perfect ring then \(\mathbf u(P)=2\).

hits.title: Additive unit representations in rings over global fields -- a survey
hits.text: Summary: We give an overview on recent results concerning additive unit representations. Furthermore the solutions of some open questions are included. We focus on rings of integers in number fields and in function fields of one variable over perfect fields. The central problem is whether and how certain rings are (additively) generated by their units. In the final section we deal with matrix rings over quaternions and over Dedekind domains. Our point of view is number-theoretic whereas we do not discuss the general algebraic background.

hits.title: Sums of units in finite rings and applications to Cayley graphs
hits.text: Summary: The question of whether a ring is additively generated by its units has been studied from several perspectives in ring theory and algebraic graph theory. In this paper, we investigate this problem for finite rings, not necessarily commutative, and relate it to the connectedness of gcd-graphs, the existence of perfect state transfer, and the solvability of certain equations over finite fields. Additionally, we discuss a generalization of this question in which only certain normalized units are allowed in the generating set. Our work intersects algebra, number theory, and graph theory, and may be of interest to a broad audience.

hits.title: Free iterative and iteration \(K\)-semialgebras
hits.text:
Let \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) denote the set of rational power series over the finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with coefficients in the semiring \(K\). Equipped with a partial star operation, this set is both a partial iteration semiring and an iterative semiring. When \(K\) is commutative, \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a partial iteration \(K\)-semialgebra and also an iterative \(K\)-semialgebra, and when \(K\) is also iterative (i.e., when \(K\) is a commutative iteration semiring) then \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is an iteration \(K\)-semialgebra. In this paper the semiring \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is characterized as: {\parindent=6mm \begin{itemize}\item[--] For a proper commutative semiring \(K\), \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a free iterative \(K\)-semialgebra on \(\Sigma\). (Theorem 7.1) \item[--] For a proper commutative semiring \(K\), \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a free symmetric iterative \(K\)-semialgebra on \(\Sigma\). (Corollary 7.2) \item[--] For a commutative semiring \(K\) every finitely generated subsemiring of which is contained in a Noetherian subsemiring, \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a free (symmetric) iterative \(K\)-semialgebra on \(\Sigma\). (Corollary 7.3) \item[--] For a strongly proper atomistic commutative semiring \(K\), \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a free partial iteration \(K\)-semialgebra on \(\Sigma\). (Theorem 8.5) \item[--] For a proper atomistic commutative semiring \(K\) which is additively generated by its units, \(K^{\text{rat}}\langle\!\langle\Sigma^\ast\rangle\!\rangle\) is a free partial iteration \(K\)-semialgebra on \(\Sigma\). (Corollary 8.6) 

\end{itemize}} The paper contains also some other results.

The clean graph of a commutative ring.
hits.text: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with identity. The authors define the clean graph \(C\Gamma(R)\) of \(R\) as the graph with \(R\) as set of vertices, and with set of edges equal to \[\{(r_1,r_2)\mid r_1+r_2\text{ is either a unit or an idempotent}\}.\] The authors relate properties of the graph \(C\Gamma(R)\) to properties of the ring \(R\colon C\Gamma(R)\) is complete if and only if \(R\) is a field or a Boolean ring. The graph \(C\Gamma(R)\) is connected if and only if \(R\) is additively generated by units and idempotents. The authors characterize rings with clean graphs of finite diameter. They investigate the genus of \(C\Gamma(R)\): The clean graph of a finite ring \(R\) is planar, that is, of genus \(0\), if and only if \(|R|\le4\). The authors characterize rings with clean graphs of genus \(1\), in the class of rings that are finite products of finite local rings.

hits.title: Theory of clean rings and matrices
hits.text:
This is a well-written and quite helpful book, which is divided into 15 chapters as follows:

Chapter 1. \textit{Strongly clean conditions}.

Here the authors mainly considered some basic properties of strongly clean conditions. In fact, in Section 1.1, they investigate certain elementary strongly clean properties. In particular, a valuable criterion for an endomorphism ring to be strongly clean is given. In Section 1.2, they develop necessary and sufficient conditions for a $2\times 2$ matrices over a local ring to be strongly clean. In Section 1.3, they continue the work with a discussion on the problem of determining when a power series ring is strongly clean.

Chapter 2. \textit{Matrices over commutative rings}.

This chapter is devoted to the study of some special kinds of matrices over commutative rings, as especially the establishment of a number of equivalent characterizations of strong cleanness of matrices over commutative rings. The authors start by investigating when a companion matrix over a ring is strongly clean. They then completely characterize an arbitrary strongly clean matrix over a commutative ring $R$, in terms of the factorization in the polynomial ring $R[t]$. Next, they develop some explicit criteria for matrices of lower ranks. Finally, the authors are concerned with a general class of commutative rings over which every finitely generated projective module is free and, in addition, they describe strongly clean matrices over such rings.

Chapter 3. \textit{Triangular and generalized matrix rings}.

This chapter mainly deals with the investigation of some properties of triangular and generalized matrix rings. Specifically, the main purpose of the current chapter is to study strongly clean properties of such sorts of rings. In Sections 3.1 and 3.2, the authors investigate sufficient and necessary conditions on an arbitrary (not necessarily commutative) ring under which the triangular matrix ring over it is strongly clean. In Section 3.3, they discuss triangular matrix rings over commutative rings and describe relatively strong cleanness with respect to the full matrix rings. Finally, in the last Section 3.4, they determine the strong cleanness for generalized matrix rings and also enrich the supply of strongly clean rings.

Chapter 4. \textit{Strong $J$-cleanness}.

Here the authors mainly explore conditions that are stronger than the aforementioned strong cleanness. Moreover, a long-standing difficult question asks whether or not strongly clean rings have stable range one. Thus, the motivation of introducing strong $J$-cleanness is to construct a natural subclass of strongly clean rings which have stable range one. Concretely, in Section 4.1, the authors examine certain elementary properties of strongly $J$-clean rings. In Section 4.2, they obtain criteria on the strong $J$-cleanness of $2\times 2$ matrices over local rings in terms of the solvability of quadratic equations (compare also with Chapter 1). In Section 4.3, the authors introduce the so-called strongly $J^{\#}$-clean matrices, and besides they then derive a few more criteria for a matrix of an arbitrary size over a projective-free ring to be strongly $J^{\#}$-clean. In the final Section 4.4, the authors discuss the unique cleanness for a ring, as this new class of rings forms a subclass of strongly $J$-clean rings.

Chapter 5. \textit{Strong nil-cleanness}.

In Section 5.1, the authors establish many interesting properties of strongly nil-clean rings which was defined by \textit{A. J. Diesl} in [J. Algebra 383, 197--211 (2013; Zbl 1296.16016)] (compare with Chapter 1). In Section 5.2, they construct various examples of such rings. In Section 5.3, they study the uniqueness for nil-clean rings. In the last Section 5.4, the authors are concerned with the strong cleanness of a single $n\times n$ matrix over a commutative ring. In this aspect, many strongly nil-clean matrices over projective-free rings are thereby provided.

Chapter 6. \textit{Classes of strongly clean rings}.

This chapter is paralleled to Chapter 1 -- notice that the notion of strongly clean rings was introduced by \textit{W. K. Nicholson} in [Commun. Algebra 27, No. 8, 3583--3592 (1999; Zbl 0946.16007)]. As already noted in Chapter 4, a long-standing difficult question is of whether every strongly clean ring has stable range 1. Likewise, one of the most important features of having stable range 1 is the cancellation of related modules from direct sums over certain rings. The problem that motivates the present chapter is to describe several subclasses of strongly clean rings with stable range 1. It is shown the well-known result that strongly $\pi$-regular rings possess this property. The authors also explore various conditions under which a ring has some other similar variants of the property strong cleanness. In addition, they determine when a ring is quasi-polar.

Chapter 7. \textit{Clean properties}.

An element of an arbitrary ring is said to be clean if it is a sum of an idempotent and a unit (often called in the existing literature an invertible element) -- notice that these rings were introduced by \textit{W. K. Nicholson} in [Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 229, 269--278 (1977; Zbl 0352.16006)]. Thus, a ring is termed clean, provided each its element is clean. Over the last ten to fifteen years, this notion has been explored intensively by too many authors from all over the world that led to its so useful generalizations and variations. This chapter outlines various properties of cleanness and its derivations.

Chapter 8. \textit{Rings generated by certain elements}.

The question that motivates this chapter is to study those rings which are generated additively by their special sets of elements (e.g., units, idempotents, nilpotents, etc.). The authors start by determining when a ring is additively generated by its two (proper) units. Precisely, in Section 8.2, the authors are concentrated with the so-called perspective rings and explore conditions on such a ring under which every regular element is presentable as a sum of two units. In Section 8.3, they study the so-named elementary divisor rings and investigate the equivalent conditions under which a commutative ring is an elementary divisor ring. This provides a large class equipped with the aforementioned property. In the final Section 8.4, the authors explore when a ring is generated by idempotent and nilpotent elements. Thereby, many nil-clean matrix rings could be obtained successfully.

Chapter 9. \textit{Weakly clean and weakly nil-clean properties}.

A ring is known to be weakly clean, provided each its element is (either) a sum or a difference of a unit and an idempotent (note that this concept was defined in the commutative case by \textit{M.-S. Ahn} and \textit{D. D. Anderson} in [Rocky Mt. J. Math. 36, No. 3, 783--798 (2006; Zbl 1131.13301)]). The motivation of this chapter is to examine the structure of such rings. Exactly, in Section 9.1, the authors establish some rather elementary but basic properties of commutative weakly clean rings. They then also study some subclasses of weakly clean rings which involve nilpotents. Furthermore, in Section 9.2, the authors are focused with the so-called weakly nil-clean rings, which rings were defined by \textit{P. V. Danchev} et al. in [J. Algebra 425, 410--422 (2015; Zbl 1316.16028); J. Algebra Appl. 15, No. 8, Article ID 1650148, 11 p. (2016; Zbl 1354.16040)]). Based on these type of results, they are able to describe in some extent weakly nil-clean rings over an arbitrary field. Next, in Section 9.3, the authors deal with the so-termed strongly weakly nil-clean rings. And finally, in Section 9.4, they found some necessary and sufficient conditions via which a ring is uniquely weakly nil-clean.

Chapter 10. \textit{Periodic and weakly periodic rings}.

In the present chapter, the authors study, almost in-depth, various ring-theoretic properties of periodic rings and some related ones. Specifically, in Section 10.1, they discuss a few more elementary properties of periodic rings. In Section 10.2, the authors are concerned with a subclass of abelian periodic rings. The commutativity of such rings is discussed as well. Further, in Section 10.3, they establish various equivalencies of the so-called uniquely $\pi$-clean rings and, moreover, the structure of such rings is completely determined in terms of periodicity. In the final Section 10.4, the authors then study when a weakly periodic ring is periodic (compare with the critical remarks stated below, as well).

Chapter 11. \textit{Conditions on zero-divisors}.

Zero-divisors occur in many situations of classes of rings. For instance, each non-trivial idempotent and nilpotent are zero-divisors. A commutative ring without non-trivial zero-divisors is just called an integral domain. In the ring of $n\times n$ matrices over some integral domains, the zero-divisors are precisely the matrices with determinant zero. In the current chapter, the authors establish a number of interesting and deep results concerning the structure of rings with certain conditions on zero-divisors.

Chapter 12. \textit{Topological structures}.

As usual, a topological space is a set endowed together with a topology on it which is a set of subsets of the topological space satisfying certain requirements with respect to their unions and/or intersections. The goal that motivates the current chapter is to discover what are the existing relations between strong cleanness and properties of the topological spaces consisting of all prime ideals or all maximal ideals of a given fixed ring. In Section 12.1, the authors find necessary and sufficient conditions under which an abelian ring is nearly clean. In Section 12.2, they discuss separate properties for the special case arising at the commutativity; namely, a commutative ring is taken and then a few different situations are examined to see what happen. In Section 12.3, the authors establish some elementary, but definitely key, properties of the so-named pm-rings (that are, mainly, commutative rings for which every prime ideal is maximal). In the final Section 12.4, they describe the existing so far fundamental work on the non-commutative version of such pm-rings and too determine equivalent conditions under which a ring is feckly clean.

Chapter 13. \textit{Rings of continuous functions}.

Here, in the present chapter, the authors' objective is to systematically study the cleanness of the ring consisting of all real-valued continuous functions on a Tychonoff topological space. Throughout this chapter, all rings are assumed to be commutative with an identity element 1 and all topological spaces are a priory Tychonoff spaces.

Chapter 14. \textit{Rings with involutions}.

In Section 14.1, the authors investigate strongly *-clean rings, and also discuss several classes of such rings. In Section 14.2, they consider the uniqueness of strongly *-clean rings and, moreover, find a criterion for a *-ring to be uniquely strongly *-clean. In Section 14.3, the authors continue their work by introducing a subclass of uniquely strongly *-clean rings and, besides, they also present many valuable examples of strongly nil-*-clean rings. In the final Section 14.4, the authors discuss a few topological spaces equipped with the property of strong *-cleanness and determine when a continuous functional ring is strongly *-clean.

Chapter 15. \textit{The generalized Drazin inverse}.

The aim of this chapter is to explore the so-called g-Drazin inverse in a Banach algebra. In fact, in Section 15.1, the authors establish various elementary background properties of the g-Drazin inverse in some Banach algebras. Further, in Section 15.2, they investigate when the sum of two g-Drazin invertible elements has g-Drazin inverse. In Section 15.3, the authors examine the g-Drazin invertibility for anti-triangular block matrices. And finally, in Section 15. 4, they explored the g-Drazin inverse of block operator matrices over an arbitrary Banach space.

Resuming furthermore, the book also contains ``Preface'', ``Notational conventions'' and ends with an almost full list of 584 references from the area stated in ``Bibliography'', as well as with a complete index of the terminology. However, there is no authors index that is needed for the sake of completeness and the reader's convenience.

In conclusion, the book under review will definitely be of some interest and importance for the people who work in these presented subjects as well as for the beginners who start their scientific carrier by working in these directions of the algebra. On this vein, there are a few new techniques and approaches in the book via which the authors attack successfully the proofs of some classical results from this branch. Besides, certain innovations in the presentation of some specific moments in the subject are also demonstrated.


Critical remarks: As noticed above, in Chapter 10 the present authors consider the classes of periodic and weakly periodic rings, but unfortunately do not succeed to show that the latter class is strictly more general -- in fact, there exists a weakly periodic ring that is not periodic: indeed, it was proved in the non-cited by the present authors publication [\textit{J. Šter}, Linear Algebra Appl. 544, 339--349 (2018; Zbl 1482.15027)], that there is a nil-clean ring (and hence weakly periodic) which is not strongly $\pi$-regular (and thus surely not periodic), as wanted.

Moreover, the authors do not have cited the article [\textit{J. Cui} and \textit{P. Danchev}, J. Algebra Appl. 19, No. 12, Article ID 2050235, 15 p. (2020; Zbl 1460.16042)], in which certain more general assertions for periodic rings are established as well as periodic rings with involutions are considered (compare with Chapter 14 above, too).

hits.title: Units generating the ring of integers of complex cubic fields
hits.text:
The author investigates the problem whether or not the ring of integers of an algebraic number field can be generated by its units. In the quadratic case if \(d\) is square-free, then \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{d}]\) is generated its units if and only if \(d=a^2\pm 1\) by a result of \textit{N. Ashrafi} and \textit{P. Vámos} [Q. J. Math. 56, No. 1, 1--12 (2005; Zbl 1100.11036)].

The main result of the paper states that if \(\alpha\) is a possibly not complex root of the irreducible polynomial \(x^3-bx-c\), then \(\mathbb Z[\alpha]\) is generated by its units if and only if there is a solution \((x,y)\) of the Diophantine equation 
\[
 x^3+bxy-cy^3=\pm 1 
\]
 such that there is a unit of \(\mathbb Z[\alpha]\) of the form \(z+x\alpha+y\alpha^2\) with an integer \(z\).

As a consequence the author shows that in pure cubic fields if \(d\) square-free, \(d\not\equiv \pm 1 (\bmod \; 9)\) then \(\mathbb Z[d^{1/3}]\) is generated by its units if and only if \(d=a^3\pm 1\) or \(d=28\).

Necessary and sufficient conditions for unit graphs to be Hamiltonian
hits.text:
Given an associative ring \(R\), the unit graph \(G(R)\) has the elements of \(R\) as the vertices and vertices \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent if \(x + y\) is a unit of \(R\). The following summary result is proved about associative rings and unit graphs. Theorem: Let \(R\) be a ring such that \(R \neq Z_2\) and \(R \neq Z_3\). Then the following are equivalent: {\parindent=6mm
\begin{itemize}\item[(a)] The unit graph \(G(R)\) is Hamiltonian. 
\item[(b)] The ring \(R\) cannot have \(Z_2 \times Z_3\) as a quotient. 
\item[(c)] The ring \(R\) is generated by its units. 
\item[(d)] The unit sum number of \(R\) is less than or equal to \(\omega\). 
\item[(e)] The unit graph \(G(R)\) is connected.


\end{itemize}}

hits.text:
The Fock functor (or exponential functor) sends complex Hilbert spaces \(H\) to symmetric Fock spaces \(\Gamma(H)\), and contractions between them to contractions between the Fock spaces. It sends direct sums to tensor products: \(\Gamma(H_1\oplus H_2)=\Gamma(H_1)\otimes\Gamma(H_2)\). Therefore, it turns direct sum systems (a one-parameter family \((H_t)\) of Hilbert spaces with associative identifications \(H_s\oplus H_t=H_{s+t}\)) into product systems (a one-parameter family \((E_t)\) of Hilbert spaces with associative identifications \(E_s\otimes E_t=E_{s+t}\)). A product system is divisible (or type I) if it is generated by its units (families \((u_t)\) of vectors that factor as \(u_s\otimes u_t=u_{s+t}\)). It is type III if it has no units. (The remaining cases are type II.) Addits (a.k.a.\ additive units) and divisibility for direct sum systems are defined the same way. Every direct sum system is divisible, and a product system is divisible if and only if it arises from a direct sum system by the Fock functor. 

A sum system is a generalization of a direct sum system, roughly speaking, a Hilbert-Schmidt perturbation of a direct sum system. Replacing for special morphisms the Fock functor with Shale's theorem, also a sum system gives rise to a product system. (Really, a sum system is a family of real Hilbert spaces, and the Fock spaces are over their complexifications.) This functional analytic description of Tsirelson's probabilistic contruction of type III product systems is due to [\textit{B.\,V.\,R.\thinspace Bhat} and \textit{R.\,Srinivasan}, Infin.\ Dimens.\ Anal.\ Quantum Probab.\ Relat.\ Top.\ 8, No.\,1, 1--31 (2005; Zbl 1069.46035)]. They also proved that product systems arising from divisible sum systems are either type I or type III.

Continuing his own work on type III systems (partly with Srinivasan), the author proves the following striking results:

Every sum system is divisible. Combined with B.\,V.\,R.\thinspace Bhat and R.\,Srinivasan's result, this shows that every product system arising from a sum system (and every generalized CCR flow) is either of type I or type III. A~necessary and sufficient condition for such a product system to be of type I is obtained.

hits.title: Sums of units in function fields. II: The extension problem
hits.text:
\textit{M. Jarden} and \textit{W. Narkiewicz} [Monatsh. Math. 150, No. 4, 327--332 (2007; Zbl 1121.12002)] considered the problem which number fields \(K\) have the property that every algebraic integer in \(K\) is a sum of units. They also proved that the ring of integers of the abelian closure of \(\mathbb Q\) is generated by its units. And even more, by the famous Kronecker-Webber theorem every abelian field is a subfield of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)\) for some \(m\), where \(\zeta_m\) is a primitive \(m\)-th root of unity. Since \(\mathbb Z[\zeta_m]\) is the ring of integers of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)\) every abelian number field \(K\) has a finite extension \(L\) namely \(L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)\) such that its ring of integers is generated by its units. This motivates the following problem:


``Has every number field \(K\) a finite extension \(L\) such that the ring of integers of \(L\) is generated by its units?''

The paper under review gives an affirmative answer to this question in case of function fields. In particular, let \(K\) be a perfect field, \(F|K\) an algebraic function field over \(K\), i.e. \(F\mid K\) is a field extension of transcendence degree \(1\), \(S\neq\emptyset\) a finite set of places and \(O_S\) the ring of \(S\)-integers in \(F\). Then there exists a finite extension \(F'\mid F\) such that the integral closure of \(O_S\) in \(F'\) is generated by its units as a ring.

For Part I see Monatsh. Math. 164, No. 1, 39--54 (2011; Zbl 1239.11123).

hits.title: On rings of integers generated by their units
hits.text: Summary: We give an affirmative answer to the following question by \textit{M. Jarden} and \textit{W. Narkiewicz} [Monatsh. A group \(G\) is said to satisfy a group identity if there is a nontrivial word \(w\) in a free group on countable letters so that any homomorphism of the free group to the group \(G\) contains \(w\). In the paper under review the authors show that a prime ring \(R\) whose unit group satisfies a group identity and which is generated by its units is either a domain or a full matrix ring over a finite field. hits.title: Submaximal integral domains
hits.text:
The author in [Far East J. Math. Sci. (FJMS) 32, No. 1, 107--118 (2009; Zbl 1164.13004)], and the author collaborating with the reviewer in [Rend. Semin. Mat. Univ. Padova 126, 213--228 (2011; Zbl 1234.13009)], [J. Algebra Appl. 9, No. 5, 771--778 (2010; Zbl 1204.13008)], [Algebra Colloq. 19, Spec. Iss. 1, 1125--1138 (2012; Zbl 1294.13007)] and [Algebra Colloq. 19, Spec. Iss. 1, 1139--1154 (2012; Zbl 1294.13008)], have initiated the study of the existence of maximal subrings in commutative rings \(R\) with \(1\neq 0\). In particular, in [Zbl 1234.13009, Zbl 1204.13008], fields and artinian rings which have maximal subrings are completely characterized, respectively. A commutative ring \(R\) with a maximal subring is called a submaximal ring.

In the article under the review, the author continues his study of latter rings and, in particular, he is interested in domains which are submaximal. In [Zbl 1234.13009], it is observed that the quotient field of any non-field domain is submaximal. In extending this result, he considers a ring \(R\), and a UFD \(D\) as a subring of \(R\) such that \(p^{-1}\in R\) for some irreducible element \(p\in D\), and in Theorem 2.2, shows that \(R\) is submaximal. Consequently, if \(D\) is any non-field UFD, then any ring containing the quotient field of \(D\) is submaximal. In particular, any ring containing the field of rational numbers is submaximal, see also [Zbl 1234.13009, Zbl 1204.13008]. In Corollary 2.19, it is shown that if \(R\) is any domain whose Jacobson radical is nonzero, then any algebra over \(R\) is submaximal which generalizes [Zbl 1294.13008, Corollary 2.24]. Consequently, he observes that for any ring \(R\), either \(R\) is submaximal or it is a Hilbert ring with \(\mathrm{Spec}(R)\leq 2^{2^{\aleph _0}}\). A ring \(R\) is called a residue finite ring if \(\frac{R}{I}\) is a finite ring for every nonzero ideal \(I\) of \(R\). In theorem 2.29, Azarang characterizes residue finite rings which are non-submaximal.

In particular, it is shown that these rings are countable principal ideal rings which are algebraic over their prime subrings.

Moreover, it is observed that if \(R\) is a residue finite ring, which is non-submaximal, then either \(\dim(R)=1\), in which case, \(R\) is a domain generated by its units, or \(\dim(R)=0\), in which case, \(R\) is artinian with nonzero characteristic, whose set of ideals is finite. As a consequence of Theorem 2.31, it's observed that if \(S\) is a multiplicatively closed subset of \(R\) such that \(R_S\) is submaximal and \(\mathrm{Max}(R_S)=\mathrm{Spec}(R_S)\) is a finite set, then \(R\) is submaximal too. Let us recall that an integral domain \(R\) is called atomic if each nonzero element of \(R\) is finite product of irreducible elements (not necessarily unique) of \(R\) (e.g., noetherian domains). The following three interesting results, of which, the third one is the main result of this article show that certain domains are submaximal.

Theorem A (Theorem 3.5). Let \(R\) be an uncountable atomic domain with zero characteristic such that every natural number has at most countably many divisors in \(R\). Then \(R\) is submaximal.

Theorem B (Proposition 3.10). Let \(R\) be an uncountable Dedekind domain whose set of maximal ideals is countable. Then \(R\) is submaximal.

The next theorem generalizes the fact that every uncountable field is submaximal, see [Zbl 1204.13008, Corollary 1.3].

Theorem C (Theorem 3.1). Every uncountable UFD is submaximal.

Reviewer's comment: Reading the following forthcoming articles together with the pertinent ones in the list of references of the article under the review, provide a good and useful background for those young students who are looking for some reasonable and rather new topics in commutative rings to do research.

\textit{A. Azarang}, ``The space of maximal subrings of a commutative rings'', to appear in Commun. Algebra, \url{doi:10.1080/00927872.2013.849264}.

\textit{A. Azarang} and \textit{G. Oman}, J. Algebra Appl. 13, No. 7, Article ID 1450037, 29 p. (2014; Zbl 1308.13012).

\textit{A. Azarang}, ``On the existence of maximal subrings in commutative noetherian rings'', to appear in J. Algebra Appl., \url{doi:10.1142/S021949881450073X}.

The first part of this article appeared in [Acta Math. Inform. Univ. Ostrav. 11, No. 1, 29--72 (2003; Zbl 1169.11306)]. In this earlier paper the author continued his investigation on Pythagorean triples, uniform distribution and applications which he already started in [Bonn. Math. Schr. 121, 1--32 (1980; Zbl 0444.10025) and in [Aequationes Math. 58, No. 1-2, 163--175 (1999; Zbl 0938.11037)]. 

In the first part of this paper the author focused on the construction of Pythagorean triples by means of prime numbers in the Gaussian number field and various geometric applications. In the first three sections of Part I applications to line geometry and to spherical trigonometry are discussed. Sections 4--6 are devoted to rotations in the three-dimensional space. 

The present second part starts with Sections 7, which is devoted to the orthogonal group in higher dimensions. Section 8 gives applications to non-Euclidean geometry and in Section 9 Clifford's surface is discussed. In Section 10 Gödel's cosmological model is considered. In Section 11 and 12 applications to a probabilistic model and to infinite series are discussed. The paper ends with several interesting remarks on solitons, Doppler's phenomenon and aberration and on extensions of the theory to quaternions and imaginary quadratic number fields.
