hits.text:
In analogy with a Pythagorean triple, the authors of the paper under review refer to an ordered quadruple \((x,~y,~z,~w)\) of integers satisfying \(x^2+y^2+z^2=w^2\) as a \textit{Pythagorean box}, or \(PB\) for short. Geomerically, when all four parameters are positive they represent a rectangular box whose three edges and inner diagonal are integers. Motivated by various composition laws that exist on the set of Pythagorean triples, the authors study composition (multiplication) laws on the set of the \(PB\)'s for which (for technical reasons) they must first assume that \(y\) and \(z\) are not simultaneously zero. The easiest way of interpreting such a composition law is identifying each \(PB\) with a suitable \(4\times 4\) matrix, and then the composition law ends up being precisely the usual matrix multiplication. Under this compositon law, the set of \(PB\)'s becomes a commutative semigroup with cancellation (i.e., the coresponding matrices are invertible).


Next they look only at the similarity classes of such \(PB\)'s, namely they consider only the projective points \([x,~y,~z,~w]\in {\mathbb P}^3_{\mathbb Q}\) which are images of \(PB\)'s. They show that the quotient of the semigroup of the \(PB\)'s under this equivalence relation is a group, and that if one allows the point \([1,~0,~0,~1]\) (which corresponds to part of the class of \(PB\)'s for which \(y=z=0\), which were not allowed in the beginning of the discussion), then one may extend the composition to include this point as well, and on the resulting set one may even define an addition operation (which is compatible with the multiplication) in such a way that the resulting structure is a field isomorphic with the field of Gaussian rationals (and \([1,~0,~0,~1]\) plays the role of the zero element here).


The remainder of the paper deals with various arithmetic properties of the \(PB\)'s. For example, by using well-known results on Pell equations the authors show how one can construct infinitely many \(PB\)'s having height \(x=1\) and square \(y=z\) base, and they remind the reader of an open problem concerning the existence of a perfect \(PB\), that is a \(PB\) for which the face diagonals are integers as well.

hits.title: Introduction to experimental mathematics
hits.source: Cambridge Mathematical Textbooks. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (ISBN 978-1-107-15613-5/hbk). xv, 303~p. (2017).
hits.text:
This book presents an in-depth analysis of the field of experimental mathematics, namely the study of mathematical theorems and concepts using computational tools. The book begins with a gentle introduction to the field via the presentation of a number of mathematical problems that can be studied with computers, such as the Tower of Hanoi, the Fermat primes, the Collatz conjecture and Pythagorean triples. The second chapter presents an introduction to the Maple programming language, which is used throughout the book for the computational experimentation. The key concepts of the language and sample programs are presented, aimed at a user without any familiarity with the language. The next chapter considers the areas of iteration and recursion in computer programs and many code samples, based on mathematical problems, are provided to expose the power of the Maple programming language.

The fourth chapter considers the visualization of the results and the creation of charts, along with simple data analysis tasks, including problems such as data transformation, linear and nonlinear fitting and the display of probability distributions. This is followed by a lengthy chapter considering the idea of symbolic inversion, looking, among others, at how one represents mathematical notions programmatically. Here, many types of problems are examined, such as continuous fractions, sequences of integers such as Fibonacci and Bernoulli numbers, graph puzzles, paradoxes due to floating-point arithmetic, generating functions and Catalan numbers.

The sixth chapter studies pseudorandomness, including the theory behind the generation of pseudo-random numbers, the Mersenne twister algorithm, Monte Carlo methods, and their use in algorithms for approximate primality testing. The last two chapters consider the important aspect of computational time and memory use as well as techniques to reduce the algorithmic complexity via efficient coding and data structures, and applications of experimental mathematics in graph theory and linear algebra, including the four color theorem.

Each chapter in this very interesting and innovative book concludes with a large list of exercises for the interested student, longer exercises for group work and notes for further reading.

hits.title: On the Existence of Algebraic Equiangular Lines
hits.abstract: We consider real and complex equiangular lines, generated by unit vectors. We show that, for an arbitrary dimension $d$, if there exists a set of $d^2$ equiangular unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^d$, then there must exist a set of $d^2$ equiangular unit vectors with all of their coefficients in a number field. This result is motivated by the question of constructing SIC-POVMs in quantum physics and conjectures around them. We discuss applications of our techniques to the case of real equiangular lines and consequences of the above results.

hits.title: On generalised Pythagorean triples over number fields
hits.abstract: Generalised Pythagorean triples are integer tuples $(x,y,z)$ satisfying the equation $E_{a,b,c}: ax^2+by^2+cz^2=0$. A significant amount of research has been devoted towards understanding generalised Pythagorean triples and, in particular, we can now determine whether $E_{a,b,c}$ has solutions and find them in a computationally effective manner. In this paper, we consider an extension of generalised Pythagorean triples to number fields $K$. In particular, we survey and extend the existing results over $\mathbb{Q}$ for determining if $E_{a,b,c}$ has solutions over number fields and if so, to find and parameterise them, as well as to find a minimal solution. Throughout the text, we incorporate numerous examples to make our results accessible to all researchers interested in the topic of generalised Pythagorean triples.

hits.title: A note on prime divisors of polynomials \(P(T^k)\), \(k\ge 1\)
hits.text: Summary: Let \(F\) be a number field, \(O_F\) the integral closure of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(F\), and \(P(T)\in O_F[T]\) a monic separable polynomial such that \(P(0) \ne 0\) and \(P(1) \ne 0\). We give precise sufficient conditions on a given positive integer \(k\) for the following condition to hold: there exist infinitely many non-zero prime ideals \(\mathcal P\) of \(O_F\) such that the reduction modulo \(\mathcal P\) of \(P(T)\) has a root in the residue field \(O_F/\mathcal P\), but the reduction modulo \(\mathcal P\) of \(P(T^k)\) has no root in \(O_F/\mathcal P\). This makes a result from a previous paper (motivated by a problem in field arithmetic) asserting that there exist (infinitely many) such integers \(k\) more precise.

It is a classical result in number theory due to Dirichlet that there exist infinitely many primes in the arithmetic progression \(kn+l\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), where \(k,l\) are given coprime positive integers. The aim of this paper is to give a simple and direct proof of this result in the case \(l=-1\) (whereas the known proofs for the general case are rather complicated, as the author recalls).

The idea of the proof is to provide an explicit family of polynomials \(\Phi_k(x)\), \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), such that they have infinitely many prime divisors (i.e., \(p\) prime such that \(p\) divides \(\Phi_k(n)\) for some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)) which belongs to the arithmetic progression \(\{kn-1\mid n\in\mathbb{N}\}\). Using the known fact that a non-constant polynomial has an infinity of prime divisors, the proof follows.

hits.title: Arithmetic progressions of polynomials over a finite field
hits.source: Yıldırım, Cem Y. (ed.) et al., Number theory and its applications. Proceedings of a summer school at Bilkent University, Ankara, Turkey. New York, NY: Marcel Dekker (ISBN 978-0-8247-1969-2/pbk; 978-1-138-40407-6/hbk; 978-0-429-33267-8/ebook). Lect. Notes Pure Appl. Math. 204, 1-21 (1999).
hits.text:
Let \(k\) be a rational congruence function field over \({\mathbb F} _q\), the finite field of \(q\) elements. The maximal abelian extension is given by the union of the fields \(N = k _n \cdot k(\Lambda _M) \cdot L _\nu\) where \(k _n\) is the constant field extension of \(k\) of degree \(n\), \(k(\Lambda _M)\) is the cyclotomic function field corresponding to the nonzero polynomial \(M\) and \(L _\nu\) is the extension of degree \(q ^\nu\) where the infinite prime is totally and wildly ramified. \(N\) is called an \((n, M, \nu)\)-extension. 


The author introduces \((n, N, \nu)\)-arithmetic progressions as certain sets of prime polynomials in \(R _T = {\mathbb F} _q [T]\) unramified in \(N\) with the same Artin symbol in \(N/k\). He finds necessary and sufficient conditions for a prime polynomial not dividing \(M\) to lie in the congruence subgroup corresponding to the abelian extension \(N/k\) and also necessary and sufficient conditions for two polynomials not dividing \(M\) to lie in the same \((n, M, \nu)\)-arithmetic progression. As an example, the author determines all the arithmetic progressions of \({\mathbb F} _3[T]\) corresponding to \(n=2\), \(\nu = 1\), \(M = T ^2\) and classifies all prime polynomials of degree \(\leq 5\) over \({\mathbb F} _3\) into their arithmetic progressions. 


Finally, let \(K/k\) be a finite Galois extension and let \(K'/k\) be the maximal abelian subextension. Then \(K'\) is contained in some \(N = k _n \cdot k(\Lambda _M) \cdot L _\nu\). The author proves that if \(C\) is a conjugacy class in \(G\), then the set \(\text{Art}_{K/k} ^{-1} (C)\) of prime divisors of \(k\) which are unramified in \(K\) with Artin symbol \(C\) in \(K/k\) has the same density in each arithmetic progression which it meets. 


Reviewer's remark: In page 12, line 9 there is a minor misprint; it should say ramified instead of unramified.

hits.title: Supersingular j-invariants as singular moduli mod p
hits.text:
Let \({\mathfrak O}_ D={\mathbb{Z}}[{1\over2}D+\sqrt{-D})]\) for \(D\equiv 0\) or 3 mod 4, and let \(P_ D(X)\) be the minimal monic polynomial whose roots are the distinct j-invariants of elliptic curves over \({\bar {\mathbb{Q}}}\) with complex multiplication by \({\mathfrak O}_ D\). The author gives several results concerning the reduction \(mod\quad p\) of the polynomials \(P_ D(X).\) 


Let E be an elliptic curve over \({\mathbb{Q}}\), and let J be its j-invariant. Then every prime p of good, supersingular reduction for E is a prime factor of the numerator of \(P_ D(J)\) for some D such that p does not split in \({\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-D})\). \textit{N. D. Elkies} [Invent. Math. 89, 561- 567 (1987; Zbl 0631.14024)] noted that D can be chosen to be \(<2p^{2/3}.\) The author shows that this bound can be improved to \(D<(4/\sqrt{3})\sqrt{p}\) as a consequence of his result that every supersingular j-invariant contained in \(F_ p\) is a root of some \(P_ D(X)\quad mod\quad p\) with \(D<(4/\sqrt{3})\sqrt{p}.\) 


The author also gives bounds on the prime divisors of the resultant of \(P_{D_ 1}(X)\) and \(P_{D_ 2}(X)\) for different discriminants \(- D_ 1\) and \(-D_ 2\). When \(D_ 1\) and \(D_ 2\) are relatively prime fundamental discriminants this is a result due to \textit{B. H. Gross} and \textit{D. B. Zagier} [J. Reine Angew. Math. 355, 191-220 (1985; Zbl 0545.10015)]. Finally, the author gives a new proof of a result, first due to Elkies, that if \(p\equiv 3\quad mod\quad 4\) then \(P_ p(X)\equiv (X- 12^ 3)(R(X))^ 2mod\quad p\) and \(P_{4p}(X)\equiv (X-12^ 3)(S(X))^ 2mod\quad p\) with R(X), S(X)\(\in {\mathbb{Z}}[X]\).

hits.title: Primes in certain arithmetic progressions
hits.text: The author proves the following theorem: A ``Euclidean proof'' exists for the arithmetic progression \(l\pmod k\) if and only if \(l^2\equiv 1\pmod k\). In other words, it is impossible to prove Dirichlet's theorem for certain arithmetic progressions by Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes.

hits.title: Hypothesis H and an impossibility theorem of Ram Murty
hits.source: Rend. Semin. Mat., Univ. Politec. Torino 68, No. 2, 183-197 (2010).
hits.text:
Let \(a\) and \(m\) be integers with \(m>0\) and \(a\) relatively prime to \(m\). Dirichlet has proved that the arithmetic progression \(a\bmod m\) contains infinitely many prime numbers. In some special cases there are proofs which parallel Euclid's argument for the existence of infinitely many primes. Can Dirichlet's theorem be proved by such ``Euclidean'' arguments? In [Sitzungsber. Berl. Math. Ges. 11, 40--50 (1912; JFM 43.0261.02)], \textit{I. Schur} showed that one can construct an argument of this type for every progression \(a\bmod m\) satisfying \(a^2 \equiv 1\pmod m\), and in [J. Madras Univ., Sect. B 51, 161--169 (1988; Zbl 1194.11093)], \textit{M. Ram Murty} showed that these are the only progressions for which such an argument can be given.

The author gives a heuristic explanation for this result by showing how it follows from Bunyakovsky's conjecture on prime values of polynomials. He also proposes a widening of Murty's definition of a Euclidean proof. He writes: ``With this definition, it appears difficult to classify the progressions for which such a proof exists. However, assuming Schinzel's Hypothesis H, we show that again such a proof exists only when \(a^2 \equiv 1\pmod m\).''

hits.title: On a theorem of Bauer and some of its applications
hits.text:
Für einen gegebenen algebraischen Zahlkörper \(K\) bedeute \(P(K)\) die Menge der rationalen Primzahlen, die einen Primidealfaktor vom ersten Grad in \(K\) haben. \textit{M. Bauer} bewies in [Math. Ann. 77, 353--356 (1916; JFM 46.0249.02)] den folgenden Satz: Ist \(K\) normal, dann folgt aus \(P(\Omega) \subset P(K)\) die Beziehung \(\Omega \supset K\). 

Hierin kann die Annahme \(P(\Omega) \subset P(K)\) durch die schwächere Voraussetzung, daß die Menge der Primzahlen \(P(\Omega) - P(K)\) endlich ist, ersetzt werden. Dies wird kurz mit \(P(\Omega) \le P(K)\) bezeichnet. Ein Körper \(K\) heißt Bauerscher Körper, wenn aus \(P(\Omega) \le P(K)\) folgt, daß \(\Omega\) mindestens einen der Konjugierten von \(K\) enthält. 

Das Theorem 1 sagt dann aus: Es seien \(K\) und \(\Omega\) zwei algebraische Zahlkörper, \(\overline{K}\) die normale Hülle von \(K\), \(\mathfrak G\) die Galois-Gruppe von \( \overline{K}\), \(\mathfrak{H}\) und \(\mathfrak{J}\) die Untergruppen von \(\mathfrak G\), die zu \(K\) bzw. zu \(\Omega \cap \overline{K}\) gehören; es seien ferner \(\mathfrak{H}_1, \mathfrak{H}_2, \ldots, \mathfrak{H}_n\) alle Untergruppen von \(\mathfrak G\), die konjugiert zu \(\mathfrak{H}\) sind. Dann ist \(K\) genau dann ein Bauerscher Körper, wenn jede Untergruppe von \(\mathfrak G\), die in \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} \mathfrak{H}_i\) enthalten ist, auch in einem \(\mathfrak{H}_i\) enthalten ist. 

Daraus ergibt sich u. a., daß alle kubischen und biquadratischen Körper Bauersche Körper sind (Theorem 2). 

Diese Ergebnisse werden zum Beweis eines Theorems 3 benutzt (für dessen umfangreichen Wortlaut auf die Originalarbeit verwiesen sei), woraus dann folgendes Korollar folgt: Sei \(K\) ein Körper, so daß der Grad von \(\overline{K}\) quadratfrei ist, \(N_{K/\mathbb Q}\) bedeute die Norm von \(K\) bezüglich des Körpers \(\mathbb Q\) der rationalen Zahlen, und sei \(f(x)\) ein Polynom mit rationalen Koeffizienten. Wenn jede arithmetische Progression eine ganze Zahl \(x\) enthält mit \(f(x)=N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\omega)\) mit \( \omega \in K\), dann ist \(f(x)=N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\omega(x))\) mit \(\omega(x) \in K[x]\).

hits.title: On a theorem of Bauer and some of its applications. II
An extension of the theorem of Bauer and polynomials of certain special types
hits.text:
In der vorangehend referierten Arbeit [Zbl 0158.30101] wurden vom zweitgenannten Verf. alle Körper \(K\) charakterisiert, für die aus \(P(\Omega) \leq P(K)\) folgt, daß \(\Omega\) einen der Konjugierten von \(K\) enthält; solche Körper wurden Bauersche Körper genannt. (Wegen der Bezeichnungen sei auf das vorangehende Referat verwiesen.) 

In der vorliegenden Arbeit wird eine Klasse von Bauerschen Körpern untersucht. Ein algebraischer Zahlkörper \(K\) hat die Eigenschaft (N), wenn es einen normalen Körper \(L\) gibt, dessen Grad relativ prim zum Grad von \(K\) ist, so daß die Komposition \(KL\) die normale Hülle von \(K\) ist. Dann wird in Satz 1 gezeigt, daß, wenn \(K\) und \(\Omega\) algebraische Zahlkörper sind und \(K\) die Eigenschaft (N) hat, aus \(P(\Omega) \le P(K)\) folgt, da \(\Omega\) einen der Konjugierten von \(K\) enthält. 

Unter Benutzung von Methoden einer früheren Arbeit von Davenport, Lewis and Schinzel [\textit{H. Davenport} et al., Acta Arith. 9, 107--116 (1964; Zbl 0126.27801)] wird folgendes Ergebnis (Theorem 3) hergeleitet: Es sei \(K\) ein Zahlkörper mit der Eigenschaft (N) und \(N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\omega)\) die Norm von \(K\) bezüglich des rationalen Zahlkörpers \(\mathbb Q\); sei \(f(x)\) ein Polynom über \(\mathbb Q\) derart, daß die Vielfachheit jeder Nullstelle von \(f(x)\) relativ prim zum Grad von \(K\) ist; wenn es in jeder arithmetischen Progression eine ganze Zahl \(x\) gibt mit \(f(x)=N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\omega)\) mit \(\omega \in K\), dann ist \(f(x)=N_{K/\mathbb Q}(\omega(x))\) mit \(\omega(x) \in K[x]\).
